what_its_for: Warfarin is a blood thinner that helps prevent dangerous blood clots from forming or getting bigger. Your doctor may prescribe it if you have an irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation), a mechanical heart valve, a history of blood clots in your legs (deep vein thrombosis) or lungs (pulmonary embolism), or if you recently had certain heart or blood vessel procedures.
how_to_take: Take warfarin by mouth, exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time. It is very important to take it at the same time every day — many people choose early evening. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor or pharmacist first.
dosing: Your dose is personalized just for you based on regular blood tests called INR (or PT/INR). This test measures how long it takes your blood to clot. Your doctor will adjust your dose up or down to keep your INR in a safe target range, usually between 2.0 and 3.0 for most conditions. Common starting doses range from 2 mg to 5 mg per day, but your dose may be different. Warfarin comes in color-coded tablets of different strengths (1 mg, 2 mg, 2.5 mg, 3 mg, 4 mg, 5 mg, 6 mg, 7.5 mg, and 10 mg) to make dosing easier.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one. Write down any missed doses and tell your doctor or anticoagulation clinic at your next visit.
storage: Store warfarin tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the tablets in their original container, away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep all medications safely out of reach of children and pets. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused or expired tablets.
what_to_avoid: FOODS: Vitamin K affects how warfarin works. Do not suddenly change how much you eat of foods high in vitamin K, such as leafy green vegetables (spinach, kale, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, and lettuce). You do not need to avoid these foods completely — just try to eat them in consistent amounts from week to week. ALCOHOL: Limit or avoid alcohol, as it can raise your bleeding risk and change your INR. MEDICATIONS AND SUPPLEMENTS: Many common medicines can interact with warfarin and raise your risk of bleeding or clotting. Always check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking any new prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. This includes aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), fish oil, vitamin E, and herbal products like garlic, ginkgo, or St. John's Wort. ACTIVITIES: Be careful with activities that could cause cuts, bruises, or falls. Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor. Wear protective gear during sports.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the nearest emergency room right away if you notice any of these warning signs of serious bleeding: unusual or heavy bleeding that will not stop (cuts, nose bleeds, gums), coughing or vomiting up blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, blood in your urine (pink, red, or dark brown urine), black, tarry, or bright red stools, severe headache, dizziness, or sudden weakness, vision changes, or pain and swelling in a joint. Also call your doctor if you become pregnant, start any new medication, get sick with vomiting or diarrhea lasting more than one day, have a significant change in your diet, or miss two or more doses in a row.
when_it_works: Warfarin begins to have an effect on your blood's clotting ability within 24 hours of your first dose, but it usually takes 2 to 7 days of regular dosing to reach its full blood-thinning effect. Because your dose needs to be fine-tuned through blood tests, you will have more frequent INR checks at the start of treatment. Once your dose is stable, your checks may be spaced out to once every 4 weeks. It is important to keep all your blood test appointments even if you feel well.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Warfarin can cause serious harm to an unborn baby, including birth defects and bleeding. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. A different blood thinner may be recommended during pregnancy. BREASTFEEDING: Warfarin is generally considered safe while breastfeeding, but always tell your doctor. ELDERLY PATIENTS: Older adults may be more sensitive to warfarin and may need lower doses. Extra care is needed to prevent falls and injuries. CHILDREN: Warfarin can be used in children but requires careful monitoring and dose adjustments. KIDNEY OR LIVER DISEASE: These conditions can affect how warfarin works in your body. Your doctor will monitor you more closely and may adjust your dose.
